findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This executes whatever the URL (or any redirect it serves) returns during image build, without an immutable version or integrity check. A compromised origin, redirect, or substituted response gains shell execution in the build environment and can persist arbitrary content into the produced image.

findings.title: Fail the image build when downloading the installer fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A transport failure from curl produces empty stdin, and the pipeline reports sh's successful exit status for an empty script. Docker therefore accepts the layer even though the intended installer never ran, producing an image missing its required installation.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This pipes mutable content fetched from a versionless external URL directly into sh. A compromised origin, DNS path, or changed installer can execute arbitrary code during image build and ship it in the image.

findings.title: Verify a pinned installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: The build follows redirects and pipes an externally supplied response directly to `sh`, with no immutable version, checksum, or signature verification. A compromised endpoint/redirect can execute arbitrary code in CI or poison the produced image.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported helper discards it and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a key intentionally stored with an empty value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in the public API
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported function discards that error and returns "", making a missing key indistinguishable from a key intentionally stored with an empty value. Every caller of this public API is forced to treat a failed lookup as valid data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in the exported helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Ignoring Load's ErrMissing makes an absent key indistinguishable from a key explicitly stored as "". Since LoadOrDefault is exported and returns only string, every caller is forced to treat a lookup failure as valid data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Run previously returned only after every result had been sent. It now starts goroutines and returns immediately, so callers can observe incomplete results or close their owned results channel after Run returns, causing the outstanding goroutines to panic when sending.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send is now detached from Run, so Run can return while sends remain pending. A caller that closes results after Run returns will panic pending goroutines with "send on closed channel"; callers also cannot rely on return meaning all jobs were processed.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Run no longer waits for any send to complete. A previously valid caller using a buffered channel can call Run, then close results and consume it; the new worker goroutines may subsequently send on the closed caller-owned channel and panic, or results may be absent when Run returns.

findings.title: Honor the supplied log tags
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public `tag` parameter promises that callers can label a log entry, but the body still only executes `println(message)`, silently discarding every supplied tag. Consumers of emitted logs therefore cannot classify entries by the requested tag.

findings.title: Preserve the original Log function type
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `Log` from `func(string)` to `func(string, ...string)` breaks existing consumers that pass or assign `logger.Log` as a `func(string)`, despite direct one-argument calls continuing to compile. This is a source-incompatible exported API upgrade.

findings.title: Restore the admin requirement for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: A session with isAdmin=false and the same tenantId now receives true, whereas the previous predicate denied it. This permits a non-admin tenant member to delete any record in that tenant; ownerId is not checked.

findings.title: Require admin and tenant match before deleting records
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes any non-admin whose tenantId matches the record tenantId, bypassing the prior admin requirement. It also authorizes an admin against a record from another tenant.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant match
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `&&` to `||` authorizes any non-admin user whose tenant matches the record, and authorizes an admin against records in any tenant. Either case bypasses the prior tenant-scoped administrator requirement for deletion.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or incomplete stored settings now become DEFAULTS instead of throwing. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and calls save, overwriting the original settings with light theme/default values rather than leaving the malformed data untouched and reporting the failure.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or invalid persisted settings previously stopped updateFontSize before save. They now become defaults, so updating `{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"bad"}` to 18 saves `{"theme":"light","fontSize":18}`, silently discarding the user's theme and making failure indistinguishable from valid default settings.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures when updating settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or partial stored settings now return the light/14 defaults. updateFontSize then changes the font size and saves them, so updating a raw value such as {"theme":"dark"} overwrites the user's dark theme with light; previously the validation error prevented any save.

findings.title: Use the reported commit for artifact lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` remains the commit resolved from `branch`, but `artifacts` are fetched from `verified`. Whenever those refs differ, a report claims one commit produced artifacts belonging to another.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` remains the requested branch's commit, but `artifacts` now come from the separate `verified` ref. When those refs differ, a report incorrectly claims verified-ref artifacts were built from the branch commit.

findings.title: Use the requested branch commit for report artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", the report claims it was built from the requested branch commit while listing artifacts from the verified ref. This changes the prior same-commit behavior and produces internally inconsistent reports.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all reversed entries rather than at most `limit`. Consequently, renderFeed's call with 20 returns more than 20 entries when the input has more than 20.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all reversed entries rather than at most `limit`. `renderFeed` passes 20 but then writes every returned entry, extending its nominal 20-item output to the full feed.

findings.title: Apply the positive limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all reversed entries instead of at most limit. In particular, renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9, but its loop then writes every returned entry into a 20-element array, growing the result beyond 20 when the input has more entries.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, this filter removes its row while the header still receives `entries.length`. The public manifest therefore advertises more entries than it contains.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are removed from rows, but the header still uses entries.length. A manifest with stale entries declares more entries than it contains, breaking consumers that use entry-count to validate or parse the rows.

findings.title: Count only rendered entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: With any stale entry, the output contains only live rows but `# entry-count` remains `entries.length`; consumers validating or preallocating from that header receive an internally inconsistent manifest.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported package API. Consumers compiled against the prior version that call ids.FormatLegacyID will fail to compile after upgrading.

findings.title: Retain the exported legacy-ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported ids package API. Deleting it instead of deprecating it makes existing downstream ids.FormatLegacyID(n) calls fail to compile after upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function from this module and is deleted rather than retained as a compatibility wrapper. Any consumer importing it from src/orders will fail to type-check or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Fail closed for non-comparable stored hashes
findings.whyItBreaks: `==` returned false for an absent or non-string `stored_hash`, letting `guard` return its 401 response. `hmac.compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when compared with values such as `None`, so this path now aborts instead of denying access.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute(input) API now throws "always fails" and returns no string, replacing the prior uppercase transformation. This makes the module's only exported operation unusable.

findings.title: Restore execute's result instead of unconditionally throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute function now fails with "always fails"; previously it returned the input uppercased.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute previously returned an uppercase string for every valid input; it now unconditionally throws, so all consumers of the exported API fail instead of receiving its declared string result.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only route
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24, so its intended "read-only" result at line 25 is unreachable.

findings.title: Allow eligible viewers to reach the read-only handler
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit previously reached handle()'s explicit "read-only" result, but is now rejected by isEligible() first. This makes the viewer-specific handler branch at line 25 unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only route
findings.whyItBreaks: Active viewers below the attempt limit previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only". This new rejection preempts handle's explicit viewer branch, returning "rejected" instead.

findings.title: Keep draft saving independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` reuses `canProceed`; an order with `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }` previously returns `"saved"` but now returns `"blocked"`. Payment may govern submitting an order, but it must not prevent persisting an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: The shared canProceed predicate now returns false for { state: "draft", payment: "missing" }. saveDraft uses that predicate at src/actions.ts:9, so a legitimate unpaid draft returns "blocked" instead of "saved".

findings.title: Do not require payment to save a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; therefore a normal `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }` order now returns `"blocked"` instead of the prior `"saved"`. Payment legitimately governs submission, not persistence of an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Load snapshot files from the selected commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For a requested non-stable channel, the snapshot reports that channel's head commit but returns files from stable, so consumers receive a self-inconsistent snapshot and may publish the wrong channel contents.

findings.title: Build snapshot files from the requested channel
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from `stable`, `commit` identifies that channel's head while `files` lists the stable commit's files. Consumers receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and can publish or inspect the wrong file set.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot's recorded commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from `stable`, `commit` records that channel's head while `files` are read from stable. Consumers therefore receive content that does not match the snapshot commit or channel.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=...)` promises callers a configurable output limit, but the body still always assigns `max_count = 10`, so `build("x", 3)` returns ten values. As a public function this ships an unusable contract even without in-repo callers.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: build("x", limit=2) still returns 10 items because the body unconditionally uses max_count = 10. The public parameter promises callers a result-size limit but silently ignores their supplied value.

findings.title: Honor the limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: `limit` promises to cap the built results, but the function still unconditionally sets `max_count = 10`; for example, `build("item", 2)` returns ten values.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: int(value) accepts zero and negative values despite the function's positive-int contract. charge('-1') therefore returns -100 rather than rejecting an invalid charge amount.

findings.title: Keep aliases for the renamed public functions
findings.whyItBreaks: The update removes the existing read_int and total module entry points. Existing consumers importing either name fail on upgrade with ImportError, and attribute callers fail with AttributeError.

findings.title: Reject zero and negative values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but its body is still int(value), so parse_positive_int("0") returns 0 and parse_positive_int("-1") returns -1. Callers cannot rely on the advertised validation.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts "0" and negative values. charge() relies on that result without another validation and produces zero or negative cent charges.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, apply_values returned a modified copy and left df unchanged. Writing through df now changes the caller-owned DataFrame, so callers that retain it for later use or comparison observe transformed values unexpectedly.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously apply_values copied df and changed only the returned DataFrame. This assignment now writes into the supplied df, so callers that retain and reuse their input observe values changed unexpectedly.

findings.title: Preserve the caller-owned DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df before applying mapping values. This change writes directly into df, so callers retaining the input now have their source data silently modified.

findings.title: Keep the CI workflow under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow YAML files in .github/workflows. This rename leaves no workflow in that directory, so pushes and pull requests no longer run npm ci, lint, or tests despite the README claim.

findings.title: Restore the CI workflow under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename removes the only workflow from .github/workflows; GitHub Actions will not execute YAML stored in docs, so lint and tests no longer run on pushes or pull requests.

findings.title: Restore the CI workflow under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow definitions in .github/workflows. This rename leaves no tracked workflow there, so the lint and test job no longer runs for push or pull_request events despite the README promise.

findings.title: Validate that parsed integers are positive
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-2")` returns `-2`, violating its public positive-integer contract; `charge` consequently returns `-200` for a negative amount.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name promises a positive integer, but the body directly parses signed i64 values and defaults parse failures to 0. Thus parse_positive_int("-1") returns -1 and parse_positive_int("0") returns 0; charge consequently produces -100 for "-1".

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name promises a positive integer, but parsing "-1" returns -1 (and invalid input returns 0). The direct consumer therefore computes charge("-1") as -100 rather than rejecting or neutralizing a non-positive amount.

findings.title: Borrow `items` in the debug statement
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns ownership of the `Vec`; the statement then drops that returned value. `items.len()` on line 3 consequently uses a moved value, producing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Remove the ownership-moving debug call
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items);` evaluates and discards an owned `Vec<String>`, moving it before `items.len()` on line 3. Rust rejects the subsequent use of the moved value.

findings.title: Avoid moving items into dbg!
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and consumes the `Vec<String>`; the subsequent `items.len()` borrows a moved value and fails with Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the pinned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: For a pinned tag that resolves differently from `latest`, this returns paths computed from `latest` while `fromRevision` remains the pinned revision. Consumers replaying the changeset as documented will apply a path set for the wrong base revision.

findings.title: Compute paths from the returned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` remains the revision resolved from `pinnedTag`, but `changedPaths` is now derived from `latest`. The exported Changeset contract says consumers replay paths on exactly `fromRevision`; paths calculated from another revision can omit changes since the pin or describe incompatible changes.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to r1 and latest resolves to r2, this returns fromRevision=r1 but paths computed relative to r2. Consumers replaying the changeset on r1, as the public Changeset contract requires, receive an incompatible path set.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`. Any execution of that query after migration fails with an unknown/no-such-column error.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any execution after upgrading will fail with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Update the query for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`. Any deployment that applies the migration will fail this query with an unknown/no-such-column error.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: This commits a bk_live credential into source and returns it to every caller of the billing client. Anyone with repository access can extract it to authenticate to the billing API, and environment-based credential rotation no longer takes effect.

findings.title: Retain failure for an unset billing key
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior missing-configuration error is removed. The exported makeClient API now returns an apparently valid client when BILLING_API_KEY is absent, so callers cannot distinguish an unconfigured deployment from one configured with credentials and may send requests using the unintended shared key.

findings.title: Restore the missing-key failure
findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient is exported and previously rejected an unset BILLING_API_KEY; it now returns a seemingly valid client with a fixed key, so callers cannot distinguish missing deployment configuration from successful client construction.

findings.title: Restore environment-backed billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: The bk_live credential is now committed to source and returned regardless of BILLING_API_KEY. This exposes a production billing secret to every repository reader and makes all deployments authenticate as the embedded account rather than their configured account.

findings.title: Restore the absent-config fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings()` returns `None` for a nonexistent path, but `startup()` now immediately indexes that value. Startup therefore raises `TypeError` instead of retaining the prior one-worker default behavior.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-config fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when the supplied config path does not exist. startup now immediately subscripts that None value, raising TypeError instead of retaining the previous default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Preserve defaults when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when path does not exist, but startup() now immediately subscripts it. Calling startup() with a missing settings path raises TypeError instead of starting with the previously supported workers=1 default.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error then returns nil. Its exported API therefore conflates a failed payment with a successful charge, allowing callers to mark or report a rejected charge as complete.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge only logs the error and returns nil at line 19. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a declined/failed payment from a completed charge and may continue as though payment succeeded.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error then returns nil. Its exported error-returning API now makes a failed payment indistinguishable from a successful charge, so callers can proceed as though payment completed.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping to the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey now uses only name. After settingsFor("tenant-a", "theme", store) caches tenant-a's value, settingsFor("tenant-b", "theme", store) returns that cached value without calling store.fetch for tenant-b. This exposes or applies one tenant's settings to another tenant.

findings.title: Scope cache keys by tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches a setting named "theme", tenant B's lookup for "theme" uses the identical key and returns A's value at the cache-hit branch without calling B's tenant-scoped store. This both exposes cross-tenant settings and returns incorrect configuration.

findings.title: Include the tenant ID in cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches `name`, a request for the same name under tenant B hits `settings:${name}` and returns tenant A's value without calling `store.fetch(tenantB, name)`. This leaks configuration across tenants and applies the wrong settings.

findings.title: Keep invalidate compatible with its exported signature
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers calling `invalidate(tenantId, name)` no longer compile. JavaScript consumers still run but pass tenantId as the sole `name`, deleting `settings:${tenantId}` rather than the intended setting and leaving stale cached data.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent calls with one unit remaining both read 1 before either await resumes, both save 0, and both return true. This reports two successful reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent calls for a SKU with one item both read the same remaining count before either save resolves. Both save the identical decremented value, update stock, and resolve true, so one unit is reserved twice.

findings.title: Serialize reservations across the persistence await
findings.whyItBreaks: With one unit loaded, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either await resumes, both save 0, and both resolve true. This records two successful reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Keep Inventory construction backward-compatible
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory is exported and previously had an implicit no-argument constructor. Existing TypeScript consumers using new Inventory() no longer compile; JavaScript consumers can still construct it but a positive-stock reservation dereferences undefined store.

findings.title: Preserve reserve's synchronous boolean contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers receive a Promise instead of boolean. Besides TypeScript failures, JavaScript conditionals such as if (inventory.reserve(sku)) now always take the truthy Promise branch, including when stock is unavailable.

findings.title: Remove the stale seconds conversion in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to its millisecond-based `sleep`. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) instead of one second; capped retries wait ~8.3 hours.

findings.title: Preserve retry delay units
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies it by 1000 before passing it to sleep(). The first retry now waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) rather than 1,000 ms, and capped retries wait ~8.3 hours rather than 30 seconds.

findings.title: Remove the stale ×1000 retry conversion
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 at `src/jobs/retry.ts:12`. The first failed attempt therefore waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms; the capped delay becomes 30,000,000 ms instead of 30,000 ms.

findings.title: Propagate the deferred Close error
findings.whyItBreaks: When Flush succeeds but os.File.Close reports a delayed write or filesystem error, Save now returns nil because the deferred Close result is discarded. Callers cannot distinguish a completed save from a failed one.

findings.title: Propagate file close failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close return value is ignored. If Flush succeeds but the OS reports a delayed write/commit failure on Close, Save now returns nil; before this change it returned that Close error.

findings.title: Propagate the deferred Close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. If Flush succeeds but Close fails, Save returns nil even though the previous implementation returned that failure, so callers are told the save succeeded.

findings.title: Include the page end index in the window
findings.whyItBreaks: range(start, end - 1) excludes end - 1, so every nonempty page loses its final row; pages of size one render empty and summarize silently omits rows.

findings.title: Iterate through the exclusive page end
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is already exclusive, so subtracting one omits index `end - 1` from every page. For example, page 0 of three rows at size 2 returns only the first row; a final one-row page is rendered empty, so `summarize` loses rows.

findings.title: Preserve the existing keyword parameter names
findings.whyItBreaks: These public definitions renamed keyword parameters (`n`/`lo`/`hi`, `total`/`size`, and `page`/`size`). Existing callers such as `page_count(total=5, size=2)` now raise `TypeError` instead of returning a result, making this an upgrade-breaking API change.

findings.title: Include the page end row
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval, but range(start, end - 1) excludes its final valid index. Thus page_window(['a', 'b'], 0, 2) returns only ['a']; render_page and summarize consequently omit rows.

findings.title: Restore the non-expired cache condition
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time below a positive TTL, so this condition fails, deletes the fresh entry, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating the job list
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the next index. For example, two adjacent done jobs leave the second one in the returned list.

findings.title: Restore the TTL validity comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Fresh entries now fall through to deletion and return null, while expired entries are returned indefinitely without deletion. A cache lookup immediately after set therefore always misses.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing shifts the next job left while forEach advances its index. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job is skipped and remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return fresh cache entries and evict expired ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate now returns an entry only after its TTL has elapsed. Fresh entries are deleted and return null, while expired entries are returned without deletion.

findings.title: Filter completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during `forEach` shifts the next job into the already-visited index. For two consecutive completed jobs, only the first is removed and the second is returned.

findings.title: Retain the empty-input result
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, reduce returns 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the previous explicit 0 result. Callers cannot use this public numeric API for empty datasets without now handling a non-finite result.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's row order
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. This changes a previously non-mutating query into one that silently reorders the caller's input, so later code using rows can observe a different order.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the prior numeric fallback 0. Callers of this exported function can no longer safely use its result in calculations or display it.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place. This changes the exported function's prior behavior and silently reorders data retained or reused by the caller.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the prior public behavior of returning 0.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver. Calling busiest now silently reorders the supplied array, whereas the prior implementation sorted a copy.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before deriving the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores [9, 100, 8] and n=1, reverse-lexical order yields cutoff 9, so the filter admits both 9 and 100 and slice returns the first 9-score player rather than the 100-score leader.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Default Array.sort() compares scores as strings. For scores 90, 2, and 100 with n=2, rankScores produces [90, 2, 100], setting the cutoff to 2; topPlayers then returns the first two input players, which can include score 2 while excluding score 100.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before reversing
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores 3, 20, and 100, the reversed result is [3, 20, 100], so n=1 sets cutoff to 3 and returns the first input player rather than the 100-score player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature verification
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` reveals how much of a supplied HMAC matches through comparison timing, allowing a remote attacker to iteratively forge a webhook signature. The base revision used `hmac.compare_digest` specifically to avoid this leak; a successful forgery reaches `processor(payload)` at app/webhook.py:16.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can return sooner for mismatching prefixes, creating a timing oracle against the HMAC signature. An attacker can use this to progressively forge a signature and reach the authenticated processor path.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using string equality makes comparison time depend on the matching signature prefix, allowing repeated requests to leak information useful for forging a webhook signature. The previous hmac.compare_digest avoided this side channel.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance changes atomic
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits and can commit the ledger entry before `_apply_balances` runs. If either balance update then fails, the transfer returns an error with a committed ledger record but missing or partial account changes, corrupting financial state. Previously all three SQL statements were in the same transaction.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger entry commits when the `with db.transaction()` block exits, before either balance update runs. If either update fails, the system retains a ledger record for a transfer whose balances were not fully applied; the two balance updates can also be left partially applied.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger entry commits when the transaction scope exits before either balance update runs. If either subsequent UPDATE fails, the system can retain an orphaned ledger entry or a source debit without the matching destination credit.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing dates
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces the prior explicit UTC calculation with process-local getters. The same instant can now produce different billing days by server timezone; for example, under UTC+08, 2026-09-09T18:00:00Z becomes 2026-09-10 instead of the previous 2026-09-09. sameBillingDay consequently reports different UTC-day instants as separate billing days.

findings.title: Keep billing-day extraction in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces the prior UTC contract with host-local getters. For example, in America/Los_Angeles, the instant 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z now produces 2025-12-31 rather than 2026-01-01, so the same billing event can be assigned a different day after deployment or across workers in different timezones.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation explicitly derived the billing date in UTC. Using local getters makes the same instant produce a different billing key on non-UTC hosts (for example, 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z is 2023-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles), changing sameBillingDay classification and persisted billing-day grouping.

findings.title: Restore tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads account X, a read for tenant B and account X finds the same memo entry and returns tenant A's Profile without calling fetchProfile. This leaks/cross-routes tenant-specific profile data.

findings.title: Include tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads account X, the profile is cached under X. A later read for tenant B and account X returns tenant A's cached profile at lines 15-16 without calling fetchProfile, leaking/misrouting tenant-scoped data.

findings.title: Keep the tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads account X, a read for tenant B and account X returns tenant A's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile. This crosses tenant boundaries and can expose incorrect tenant data.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a stored empty value. `loadAll` therefore returns a seemingly valid array containing empty strings instead of reporting absent required keys.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: An absent key now returns "", which is also a valid stored Map value, instead of throwing `missing: <key>`. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking data with empty entries rather than reporting that loading failed.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. loadAll consequently returns partial-looking successful data instead of propagating the missing-key failure.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config shape
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers of retry using the prior required { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } object no longer compile because timeoutMs was removed and retries is newly required. Existing JavaScript callers leave config.timeout undefined; Date.now() + undefined is NaN, so the deadline guard is always false and attempts continue past the configured timeout.

findings.title: Expose retryBackground exhaustion failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When every fn invocation throws, the catch discards every exception and the function falls through with the same void result as a successful invocation. Public callers cannot distinguish completed work from exhausted retries.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for the exported Config shape
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers of the exported retry API that pass `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check: `timeoutMs` was removed while both `timeout` and unrelated `retries` became required.

findings.title: Expose terminal retryBackground failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When every callback invocation throws, this catch discards every exception and the function returns `undefined`, exactly as it does after a successful callback. As an exported API, callers are forced to treat failed work as success.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config timeout contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check because retries and timeout are required. JavaScript callers retain timeoutMs but config.timeout is undefined, producing a NaN deadline, so the timeout guard never stops retries.

findings.title: Expose retryBackground failure to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is discarded. After retry exhaustion or deadline, retryBackground returns void exactly as it does after success, forcing users of this exported API to treat failed work as successful work.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now publicly accepts `number`, but `number` has no `length` property. TypeScript rejects this component; if transpiled without typechecking, `<Field value={123} />` renders `len=undefined` instead of a numeric-length label.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported FieldProps contract now permits number, but number has no length property. Type checking rejects this expression; transpile-only consumers render `len=undefined` for a numeric value.

findings.title: Convert numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now publicly accepts numbers, but numbers have no `length`. TypeScript rejects this expression; transpile-only consumers instead render `len=undefined` for every numeric value.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer drops spawnSync to Node's 1 MiB default. The full PR patch is captured by git diff at line 140; a diff between 1 MiB and the previously supported 64 MiB exceeds that limit, causing git() to throw before review posting begins.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The patch is read through this helper at line 140, so a PR with a diff over 1 MiB terminates git diff and aborts the review instead of producing a result. The prior 64 MiB limit explicitly supported these inputs.

findings.title: Preserve the Git diff output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. git() reads the complete PR patch at line 140; patches between 1 MiB and the previous 64 MiB limit now return a buffer-overflow result, which this function turns into an exception before runGithub reaches its error reporting/check-posting path.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` lets Codex select a writable sandbox through its configuration. Since the process runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, prompt-injected model commands can modify or delete files in the checkout being reviewed rather than being prevented by the wrapper.

findings.title: Keep Codex executions read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` delegates the sandbox policy to the Codex CLI default/configuration. Since this process receives the review prompt on stdin and runs with `cwd` set to `opts.repoPath`, a write-capable policy lets model instructions or prompt-injected repository content create, alter, or delete files in the repository being reviewed. The prior explicit policy prevented that mutation path.

findings.title: Restore the read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The child process runs with cwd set to opts.repoPath, but no longer overrides Codex's configured sandbox mode. A workspace-write or danger-full-access configuration can therefore let the prompt-driven Codex process alter files in the repository being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore merge-base/head range for the review bundle
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `baseSha..HEAD` compares the current base tip directly with the checkout. If `PR_BASE_SHA` is newer than the commit from which the PR head forked, the diff includes base-only changes, so `review(bundle)` can review and comment on changes not made by the PR. It also ignores the resolved `PR_HEAD_SHA` while reviews/checks are posted to that SHA.

findings.title: Keep the diff rooted at the PR merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is a target-branch tip that advanced after the PR branch forked, it is not an ancestor of HEAD. `git diff baseSha HEAD` then includes target-only commits as reverse changes, and changedFiles includes their paths. The reviewer can report base-branch changes as PR changes and attempt invalid inline comments.

findings.title: Restore merge-base diffing for PR reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: When a PR branch was created before its base branch advanced, baseSha is not an ancestor of the PR head. Comparing baseSha directly to HEAD includes base-only commits as apparent deletions/changes, so review() receives and can report on files not changed by the PR. It also ignores the configured PR_HEAD_SHA in favor of the checkout commit.

findings.title: Preserve prompt payloads during interpolation
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace` interprets `$&`, `$`` , `$'`, and `$$` in a string replacement. A reviewed patch containing (for example) `$&` is inserted as the `{{PATCH}}` token rather than literal patch content; other tokens can duplicate surrounding prompt text. The same regression affects serialized bundles and findings, causing the review/critic models to receive corrupted context.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets $-substitutions in a string replacement. A PR patch or model finding containing `$&` causes the matched placeholder (for example `{{PATCH}}`) to be inserted instead of the literal payload; `$`` and `$'` can duplicate prompt sections. The review and critic stages can therefore receive malformed or missing PR content.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences in prompt inputs
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace treats `$&`, `$$`, `$`` and `$'` in string replacement arguments specially. A PR patch or bundle containing `$&`, for example, inserts the matched placeholder instead of the literal patch content; the same corruption affects candidate findings and the patch passed to the critic. The review model can consequently receive a materially altered diff or context.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the JSON review request fails (for example, due to an invalid inline comment), this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then uses the PR's latest commit rather than headSha, which was the SHA diffed and reviewed. If a push arrives during the review, the fallback can publish this verdict against code that was never reviewed.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews bound to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: If the PR head advances after the bundle is built, the initial request correctly fails because its commit_id is the now-stale headSha. The catch then retries without commit_id, which GitHub applies to the latest PR commit, publishing a pass or change-request verdict derived from the old patch against unreviewed code. Previously the retry also used headSha and failed rather than misattributing the review.

findings.title: Pin fallback reviews to the reviewed head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: If the initial POST fails (for example, due to an invalid inline comment) and a new commit is pushed before the fallback POST, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's then-latest commit rather than headSha. The check run remains attached to headSha, so an unreviewed newer revision can receive the review verdict.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: An invalid severity such as "P9" previously threw; it now becomes a legitimate P1 finding. Missing required fields likewise become empty strings or zero line numbers, so normalizeReview returns malformed producer output with no remaining error signal for consumers to distinguish from a real finding.

findings.title: Preserve the strict review-normalization API
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported strict parameter breaks TypeScript callers of normalizeReview(raw, false). JavaScript callers using false also change behavior: malformed entries were filtered, but are now retained as fabricated default findings.

findings.title: Restore rejection of malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing required fields now produce a returned Finding with values such as file="" and lineStart=0; invalid severities and categories become P1/bug. Callers cannot distinguish malformed review output from a genuine finding, whereas strict normalization previously propagated the validation error.

findings.title: Preserve the public strict-mode option
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers calling normalizeReview(raw, false) no longer compile. Emitted JavaScript callers silently have the extra argument ignored and now receive fabricated default findings instead of the prior behavior of dropping malformed entries.

findings.title: Reject malformed finding fields instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: An invalid finding such as one with severity "critical" formerly raised a validation error in the default path. It now returns a P1/bug Finding, with absent locations represented as an empty file and line 0. normalizeReview receives no error, so consumers cannot distinguish malformed review output from a real finding.

findings.title: Restore the public strict parsing mode
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, false) was a public supported mode that caught malformed entries and returned the valid entries. The removed parameter now makes TypeScript consumers fail to compile; JavaScript consumers have their second argument ignored, and findings:[null] reaches raw.severity and throws instead of being filtered.

findings.title: Pass the repository explicitly when resolving manual dispatch refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, pull_request SHAs are absent, so this branch runs before the first checkout. gh pr view without --repo/-R resolves its repository from a local git repository or GH_REPO; neither exists here after removing REPO. The manual PR-number path therefore cannot retrieve the requested head/base refs.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository for manual PR ref lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before any checkout. Removing -R leaves gh pr view without a repository source; a fresh runner workspace has no checked-out git remote to infer it from. The ref lookup fails (or can use stale self-hosted workspace state), leaving empty/wrong checkout SHAs and breaking manual reviews.

findings.title: Pass the target repository when resolving manual-dispatch PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and this branch runs before any checkout. Without -R (or GH_REPO), gh pr view has no guaranteed repository context in a fresh runner workspace, so it cannot obtain the selected PR's head/base SHAs and the manual review workflow cannot review that PR.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Payloads missing required review fields now become a valid-looking RawReview with empty findings and risks instead of throwing. A caller cannot distinguish invalid model output from a legitimate empty review.

findings.title: Reject malformed review envelopes
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs that previously threw protocol-validation errors, such as a response missing findings, checked, or residual_risks, now normalize to empty arrays and an empty summary. This makes an invalid reviewer response indistinguishable from a successful review with no findings, so public callers can accept and report the fallback instead of surfacing the failed review.

findings.title: Restore errors for malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null or a payload missing findings previously threw a malformed-review error; they now become a structurally valid review with empty findings, checked, and residual risks. The exported API therefore forces consumers to conflate invalid model output with a legitimate empty review.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch has only pr_number and no pull_request payload. These expressions therefore select github.ref (the manually selected workflow branch) for checkout and pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA values, rather than the requested PR's head and base. A manual review can consequently execute the wrong revision and lacks the PR commit bounds.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR before manual checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout therefore falls back to github.ref (the branch used to dispatch the workflow, not input pr_number), fetches main rather than the PR's actual base branch, and supplies empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA values. Manual runs consequently review/run the wrong revision instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR head for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so this falls back to github.ref: the branch selected to run the workflow, not the required pr_number. Dispatching from main for any PR therefore installs and runs the main revision rather than the requested PR's source, contradicting the manual trigger's stated review contract.

findings.title: Retain a buffer sufficient for patch output
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` reads the entire `git diff` at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses Node’s 1 MiB default; a larger patch exceeds it, returns a failed result, and this helper throws instead of producing a review. The previous 64 MiB limit supported such patches.

findings.title: Restore the 64 MiB buffer for diff capture
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal captures the complete base-to-HEAD patch at line 100. Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default; a larger diff terminates git with a max-buffer error and this helper throws, so the review cannot run. The prior implementation explicitly supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore the git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. runLocal obtains the entire PR patch via git diff at line 100, so any diff exceeding that size is terminated with ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER and the local review cannot run.

findings.title: Fail closed when review execution errors
findings.whyItBreaks: An exception from review/posting is now sent as a neutral GitHub check rather than failure. GitHub treats neutral required checks as passing, so a branch protection rule requiring the Needlefish check can allow a PR through despite the explicit "did NOT pass" review error.

findings.title: Scope PR diff to the requested repository
findings.whyItBreaks: gh pr diff resolves its repository from the process working directory because neither --repo nor cwd is supplied. If runGithub receives a checkout path different from process.cwd(), its metadata is fetched from GITHUB_REPOSITORY but its patch can come from another repository's PR with the same number (or fail), producing an invalid review bundle.

findings.title: Keep reviewer failures as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: A thrown review now posts a completed Check Run with conclusion "neutral". GitHub considers neutral required checks successful, so a repository requiring the Needlefish check can permit merging even though the review failed and the summary says it did not pass.

findings.title: Bind the PR diff to GITHUB_REPOSITORY
findings.whyItBreaks: The API metadata and review posting explicitly target GITHUB_REPOSITORY, but `gh pr diff` has neither `--repo` nor a supplied cwd. gh therefore resolves its repository from the process working directory, which can differ from the `cwd` checkout passed to runGithub; it can fetch the same PR number from another repository or fail, then post that review against the target repository.

findings.title: Report review execution errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a neutral required check as successful. A thrown review/posting error still sets the process exit code, but repositories that require the explicit Needlefish check can merge even though its review never completed; this also contradicts the emitted "did NOT pass this PR" result.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out repository contains neither package.json/pnpm-lock.yaml nor src/cli.ts. The install step cannot provide tsx, and this command consequently cannot invoke the reviewer, so every review job fails.

findings.title: Keep reviewer execution out of the PR checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow resolves and checks out the PR head, then installs and executes its package and src/cli.ts with a write-capable GITHUB_TOKEN on a self-hosted runner. A same-repository PR can alter the reviewer or package lifecycle to suppress findings or execute arbitrary code with those credentials; the removed separate checkout prevented this.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore a checkout that contains the reviewer tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out HEAD contains neither package.json nor pnpm-lock.yaml (nor src/cli.ts). Consequently pnpm install --frozen-lockfile fails before a review can run for every eligible PR or manual dispatch.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout independent of the PR
findings.whyItBreaks: This now executes src/cli.ts from the PR head. A same-repository PR can alter that code to suppress findings or use the supplied GH_TOKEN, which has pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions. The previous workflow deliberately executed the separately checked-out trusted tool instead.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The command executes src/cli.ts from the PR-head checkout. A same-repository PR can replace that file (and its locked dependencies) to run arbitrary commands on the self-hosted runner and use the write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN to forge review/check output, bypassing the review gate.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the reviewer source
findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out head tree contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no src/cli.ts. This command therefore cannot start the reviewer, so every workflow run fails rather than publishing a review.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Canonicalize severity before validating it
findings.whyItBreaks: A raw finding with severity " p2 " or "p2" now fails the exact-membership check and is emitted as P3. Previously normalizeFinding trimmed and uppercased this input, producing P2. normalizeReview passes untyped parsed findings directly to this function, so this changes externally supplied review classifications.

findings.title: Restore canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw review JSON and forwards each finding here. Values previously accepted as P1, such as "p1" or " P1 ", now fail the exact enum check and are emitted as P3; omitted severity is also downgraded from P1 to P3. This can understate a review finding's urgency.

findings.title: Keep canonicalizing severity strings before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped JSON and passes each finding to this function. A formerly accepted severity such as " p0 " or "p1" is no longer trimmed/canonicalized; it fails the exact-membership check and is silently emitted as P3, downgrading the finding.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of Codex's environment
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env option, spawnSync inherits process.env. This passes GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN to the Codex process; prompt or repository instructions can cause an agent with access to that environment to disclose or misuse credentials. The base implementation explicitly removed these values.

findings.title: Restore GitHub-token scrubbing for Codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env, spawnSync inherits process.env, exposing GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN to the Codex process. A prompt or repository instruction processed by Codex can cause those credentials to be read and included in its returned output; the base implementation explicitly prevented this.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit sanitized env, spawnSync inherits process.env. Codex and commands it invokes can now read GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, exposing repository credentials to the agent/prompt execution path.

findings.title: Block fork PRs from the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the repository-origin condition allows any fork PR to trigger this self-hosted job. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled head SHA and executes its dependency installation and src/cli.ts, granting untrusted contributors arbitrary code execution on the runner.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the same-repository condition allows a fork PR's head SHA to be checked out and then executed via `pnpm install` and `tsx src/cli.ts` on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can alter install hooks or the reviewed source to run arbitrary commands in that runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for self-hosted execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now reach the checkout of their head SHA and then execute `pnpm install` and `tsx src/cli.ts` on a self-hosted runner. An attacker can add lifecycle scripts or altered source to a fork PR and execute arbitrary commands in the runner environment.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner delays
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing deployments using either runner delay environment variable as "0" lose that explicit configuration: the new predicate returns the fallback (5000ms grace or 2000ms give-up delay). A timed-out runner that previously advanced immediately to SIGKILL or completion will now remain pending for those fallback delays.

findings.title: Continue accepting zero-millisecond runner durations
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 scheduled SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM; it now falls back to 5000ms, so configured no-grace timeouts wait five seconds. Likewise, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now adds the 2000ms fallback wait.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration configuration values
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 caused SIGKILL to follow timeout-triggered SIGTERM immediately, and setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 immediately stopped waiting after SIGKILL. Both now silently fall back to 5000ms and 2000ms respectively, breaking existing zero-duration configuration and extending timeout handling by seconds.

findings.title: Restore coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large bundles deep-review only the first six mapped hotspots. A changed file omitted by the mapper or placed in a later hotspot is never sent to a deep pass and produces no blocking risk, so the review can appear complete without examining that file.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Residual risks returned by successful deep passes are discarded and replaced with an empty array before the critic runs. In particular, a deep pass's blocks:true risk is no longer visible to the final review, allowing an incomplete review to be returned without that blocker.

findings.title: Preserve partial results when a deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A throw from any individual deep run, JSON extraction, or normalization now rejects the entire large review. Previously the other hotspots were retained and the failed surface was reported as a blocks:true residual risk, so one malformed or failed model response did not make the review unavailable.

findings.title: Restore deep coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six hotspots are reviewed. Without the removed coverage backstop, any changed file omitted from those selected hotspots is never included in a deep-review prompt, so defects in it can be silently missed.

findings.title: Keep reviewing after one deep-pass failure
findings.whyItBreaks: A runCodex, JSON extraction, or normalization failure for one hotspot now rejects the exported review() call and skips every remaining hotspot. The prior path continued reviewing and represented the incomplete hotspot as a blocking residual risk.

findings.title: Forward residual risks from deep passes
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep review can return residual risks, including blockers, but the merged candidate now substitutes []. The critic consequently receives the same input for “no risks” and “risks were found but discarded”, allowing a known blocker to disappear from the final review.

findings.title: Keep rationale in the deduplication key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two distinct findings at the same file, line, and category with matching first 60 title characters now share a key even when their explanations describe different defects. The Map retains only one, whereas the previous key preserved distinct `whyItBreaks` values.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: For a large bundle whose mapper returns more than six hotspots, `slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` excludes the remaining hotspots. Removing the uncovered-file tail means their changed files receive no deep review, so defects in those files can be omitted from the final review.

findings.title: Return a blocked result when a deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A failed Codex call or malformed deep-pass response now escapes the per-hotspot loop and rejects `reviewLarge`, skipping the critic and returning no ReviewResult. Previously this path produced a blocking residual risk while preserving results from other hotspots.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: A successful deep pass can report `residual_risks` with `blocks: true`, but the merged review now always serializes an empty array to the critic. The critic cannot distinguish an unresolved blocking review from a clean one, allowing its verdict to omit the block.

findings.title: Restore focus interpolation for large-patch reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted replacement leaves the `{{FOCUS}}` token in the deep-review prompt and never supplies `bundle.focus`. Consequently, a focused review request works on the small-review path (which serializes the whole bundle) but is ignored for every large patch.

findings.title: Preserve focus and deep options for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path strips focus and deep before creating the map prompt; it also no longer injects focus into each deep prompt. reviewSmall still serializes the full Bundle, so a caller's requested scope/depth works for small patches but is silently ignored once isLarge selects reviewLarge.

findings.title: Restore focus interpolation for deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: For bundles routed to reviewLarge, the deep prompt no longer substitutes bundle.focus, so each reviewer receives the literal {{FOCUS}} placeholder rather than the requested review scope. The map payload also omits focus. A focused large review (for example, authorization-only) is therefore treated as unfocused, while reviewSmall still supplies the complete bundle.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, minutes is floored to 1 while the remaining 59.5 seconds rounds to 60, so rendered review stats show "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". Durations from 59500ms through 59999ms similarly display as "60s" rather than rolling into one minute.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For a 119500ms stat, minutes is computed as 1 before the remaining 59500ms rounds to 60 seconds, so rendered review output reports `1m 60s` rather than the rounded duration `2m 0s`.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, this computes minutes=1 and seconds=60, so rendered stats show "1m 60s" instead of the correctly rounded "2m 0s". Values from 59500ms through 59999ms similarly render as "60s" rather than rolling into one minute.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function name and error text promise a positive integer, but the changed predicate accepts "0" and returns 0. Consumers relying on this parser to reject non-positive values can now receive an invalid value.

findings.title: Reject zero to preserve the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", ...)` now returns `0`, while both its exported name and thrown error promise a positive integer. Public callers can rely on this parser to reject zero before using its result in a positive-only setting.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, although its exported name and error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers can therefore receive an invalid zero value while relying on validation.
